title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China’s grip on critical materials with AI
description: Scimplify's annualized revenue run rate has tripled to $200 million as it eyes U.S. expansion.
content: As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense and energy emerging as key growth markets. The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation. The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process. In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview. Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch. “Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.” Scimplify’s Scinode Image Credits: Scimplify Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries. About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said. The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Simplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago. Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said. Energy, electronics and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry. Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China. The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project. With its latest funding, Scimplify plans to deploy around $7.5 million for its U.S. expansion, including building out its manufacturing network, Santhosh said. It also earmarked another $2 million for further development of Scinode. The startup employs about 340 people, including roughly 70 scientists. Most of its workforce is based in India, though it also has local teams in the U.S., Japan, Indonesia, and the UAE. fingerprint: google deepmind and singapore government announce new ai tool to protect citizens against scams|deepmind.google/blog/on-device-ai-scam-detection-mddi
title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government announce new AI tool to protect citizens against scams
description: Learn how Google DeepMind and GovTech Singapore uses lightweight on-device Gemma models to intercept conversational scams in private chats with zero cloud data egress.
content: October 14, 2026 Responsibility & Safety Google DeepMind and Singapore Government announce new AI tool to protect citizens against scams JJ Geewax and Miguel de Andrés The collaboration delivers an on-device scam detection model that helps protect citizens without compromising privacy. Scams make up over half of Singapore’s reported crimes, and account for more than S$4 billion in losses since 2019. At the same time, scam tactics have shifted from simple phishing to complex social engineering, whereby attackers manipulate victims with convincing conversations before requesting money. Such scams now account for up to 80% of all losses. To address this, Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) have been working together as part of our National AI Partnership with the Singapore Government. This has allowed us to deliver an on-device scam detection model - optimized to run on typical smartphones in Singapore - to tackle an urgent safety challenge while preserving citizens' privacy. On-device AI protection without compromising privacy Generic models often struggle with localised deception techniques, making scam detection harder. To address this, Google DeepMind's lightweight Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations. These ranged from impersonations of public institutions, banks, and local figures, to trending regional schemes, ensuring the model can distinguish benign social chatter from genuine manipulation. This new model also processes conversation data on the device. Traditionally, threat detection relies on server-side scanning of messages in the cloud, but many messaging platforms are end-to-end encrypted - meaning they cannot inspect private conversations. People need a way to stay safe from fraud at the same time as keeping conversations private, and our solution is to bring the threat analysis to the device. This allows faster analysis of conversation patterns to detect manipulative intent and allow citizens to act before financial or credential exposure can occur. Fighting scams shouldn't mean sacrificing personal privacy. Working with Google DeepMind, we're bringing advanced AI protection directly onto citizens' devices. This allows us to catch highly targeted, local scam attempts in real time while keeping personal communications completely private. Mark Chen Director, Trust and Safety, GovTech Singapore Under the hood: local context and edge efficiency When the model detects manipulative conversational patterns, it triggers a real-time warning directly on the user's device advising them to pause and exercise caution before sharing sensitive information or funds. Running a complex scam classifier model on modern smartphones is no easy task, with battery efficiency being a critical area of concern. To do this we're relying on a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1: A lightweight, efficient classifier screens inbound messages, using minimal power, focused on catching potential threats. Stage 2: Contextual evaluation with our fine-tuned Gemma model, where we analyze a larger snapshot of the conversation to confirm a threat or discard a false alarm. Built on strict governance Presented at Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW 2026), this collaboration provides a model for messaging platforms balancing user protection with end-to-end encryption. Strict governance was maintained throughout development: Sovereign Sandbox: Fine-tuning took place within GovTech's managed and maintained GCP environment, keeping training data isolated. No Citizen Data: Training strictly excluded private or personally identifiable information, utilising anonymised datasets derived from scam reports and intelligence feeds. Stress-Testing: The model was tested against synthetic dialogues and local corpora to cover diverse scam categories and evolving impersonation tactics. The future of on-device safety The project demonstrates how AI can help messaging services counter criminality and shows safety nor privacy need be compromised by running protective AI directly on-device. It also shows how governments and model providers can work together to build tech for public good. Messaging platforms and operating system vendors can directly integrate these lightweight models to safeguard users locally, ensuring chat interactions remain secure without exposing private data.
